questions.learningObjective: identify starvation and its remedies
questions.stem: Examine configuration 3501. A priority scheduler always dispatches the highest-priority ready process, and a stream of high-priority jobs arrives continuously. What problem does this create for a low-priority process that is already in the ready queue?

options.text: The low-priority process can starve indefinitely because it is never the highest-priority ready job
The low-priority process automatically has its priority raised each time it is passed over
options.misconception: assumes aging is present without being told it is configured

options.text: The low-priority process is guaranteed service because round robin rotates among all ready jobs
options.misconception: assumes a time slice is applied when this policy is purely priority ordered

options.text: The low-priority process causes a deadlock with the high-priority jobs
options.misconception: confuses indefinite postponement with a circular wait for resources

questions.explanation: Strict priority scheduling with a continuous supply of higher-priority work can postpone a lower-priority process forever. This is starvation, not deadlock, because the low-priority process holds no resource that others need. The standard remedy is aging, which gradually raises the priority of a process that has waited a long time.

options.misconception: treats a known algorithmic anomaly as a device fault

options.text: The process must have changed its reference string between the two measurements
options.misconception: explains the result by an unstated change rather than by the replacement policy

options.text: This is Belady's anomaly: FIFO can fault more with more frames because a newly loaded page can be evicted before an older one
This is impossible, because adding a frame can never increase faults under any policy
options.misconception: assumes every replacement algorithm is stack algorithms and ignores FIFO's exception

options.misconception: assumes the memory management unit performs disk I/O by itself

options.misconception: treats a legitimate demand-page miss as a protection violation

A protection fault, by contrast, is an illegal access and is handled differently.

options.misconception: confuses copy-on-write with a parent-child synchronisation rule

options.misconception: treats a protected write as a no-op rather than a trap

options.misconception: forgets that the pages are protected and ignores the copy-on-write mechanism

questions.stem: Review setup 3510. A system is known to be free of the condition called circular wait. Which statement about deadlock is correct?

A deadlock can still occur if two processes request the same resource at once
options.misconception: ignores which condition was removed and why it blocks the cycle

options.text: Removing one condition only slows deadlocks down but cannot prevent them
options.misconception: understates the role of necessary conditions

options.text: A deadlock is guaranteed because the other three necessary conditions always hold
options.misconception: forgets that every one of the four conditions is required

questions.stem: System 3512 is under study. In the dining philosophers problem, 4 philosophers sit around a table with one fork between each pair, and each philosopher needs both neighbouring forks to eat. Which condition explains the classic deadlock where nobody eats?

options.misconception: names a necessary condition but ignores the hold-and-wait cycle

options.misconception: describes a behaviour that would actually prevent the deadlock
